# Google X's 'Monkey First' Principle for De-risking Moonshots

**Source:** https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeKAwyEsCVq/ · **Type:** Reel · **Author:** Jay Barrow · **Saved:** 2026-10-07

## Summary

Google's moonshot factory (X) evaluates high-uncertainty initiatives using a framework called 'Monkey First'. Teams tackle the hardest, highest-risk challenge before investing time and capital into building predictable supporting components.

## Transcript and on-screen text

Google's secret: "Monkey First". The smartest thing Google's moonshot factory does is try to kill its own projects. It involves a monkey, a pedestal, and Shakespeare. Stick with me. Who's fixing the world? #7. This is part seven of a series ranking the teams solving our biggest problems. Imagine someone asks you to get a monkey to recite Shakespeare while standing on a pedestal. The tempting place to start is the pedestal because you know how to build it. Every day it gets a little taller, so you feel like you're making progress. In real life, this looks like hiring a team, raising money, and building the parts of a prototype you already know will work. But all this happens before answering the one question the whole thing depends on: can the monkey actually talk? So X, Google's moonshot factory, built that question into how it works. These are the people who take massive ideas like self-driving cars or making fuel from seawater and ask, could we actually make this work? But when you're attempting things nobody knows how to do yet, you could spend years on an idea that was never going to work. So they start with the thing most likely to kill it. They call this monkey first. Before you pour resources into the parts you already know how to build, test the part you're least sure you can pull off. Find the smallest, cheapest experiment that can actually answer that question. And if the monkey can't talk, stop. If it can, you've got a reason to keep building. And they actually kill incredible work. One project called Foghorn was trying to make that liquid fuel from seawater. And they pulled it off; they made the fuel. But the monkey here was whether they could make it cheaply enough. They couldn't see a viable way to get the cost there. So even after proving the tech worked, they stopped the project, which is a pretty wild decision after you figured out how to do something like that. But the alternative is spending years building shit out and hiring people only to run into the same problem. But some ideas do make it through. Google's self-driving car project grew up at X and eventually became Waymo. Wing's delivery drones came out of X as well. And that's the dope idea behind the moonshot factory. You hear moonshot and you picture throwing a massive amount of money at a crazy idea. But they keep the bets small while uncertainty is high. And as the evidence comes in, uncertainty drops, and they put more people and money behind it. Stop what doesn't work early, and you can afford more big swings. That's why they earn a seat on the Roe index. Follow to see who makes the list. Catch you next time.
